In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IRBOs are not a homogenous group of organizations, and that there are many ways of organizing transboundary water cooperation.
there are many types of IRBOs, which can be categorized in a number of ways, and which are distributed across a wide variety of basins and scales.
the most common type of IRBOs are those that have a mix of responsibilities and are not limited in their scope to a single basin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the world is not short of IRBOs but rather short on IRBO effectiveness.
IRBOs can be divided into three types based on the degree of institutional autonomy and authority they have: facilitative, autonomous and hybrid.
there is no single ‘best practice’ IRBO, but rather a range of options that are better suited for particular basins, depending on their characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no one-size-fits-all solution for IRBO design.
IRBOs are not a homogenous category.

the IRBO landscape is more complex than previously thought and the choice of IRBO type should be informed by the specific context of a transboundary water system, and the needs and interests of the basin states.
